A habit I am trying to cultivate is that when people are impressed with something I've done and the felt sense of why I can do it and they can't is that this stuff just isn't hard and I don't understand why people struggle at it, I try to identify a specific ability involved.
↓
1311576615055495169 [2020-10-01] @GeniesLoki 💜 7
Often I start with something that feels like the answer is "I'm just really clever" and end up with something where it feels like people could totally train this ability if they wanted.
↓

https://t.co/qHnlGr4FZK

1311576618360549379 [2020-10-01] @GeniesLoki 💜 6
People were like "wtf how did you come up with this many questions?" and I tongue-in-cheek answered "I'm very clever".

This is a kind of inverted version of https://t.co/nZrlQAQMsO

I actually am very clever, sorry. I took CON as a dump stat.
  [Quoting @GeniesLoki: In this tweet I will grant you a super power of great insight, at the low low cost of becoming *intensely* annoying to hang out with:  Every time tells a self-deprecating joke, they mean it literally and are pointing to a deep-seated insecurity they hope you won't notice.]
↓
1311576619983802369 [2020-10-01] @GeniesLoki 💜 7
But seriously the initial answer to this is that I just... do? I reach into the part of me where questions come from and then I ask the question.
↓
1311576621250424833 [2020-10-01] @GeniesLoki 💜 5
But asking questions seems like a skill one can totally cultivate. I don't even know if it's actually cleverness or whether it's pure cultivated talent for me: It mostly comes from years of being interested in things and trying to understand them.
↓
1311576622533926914 [2020-10-01] @GeniesLoki 💜 7
The easiest way to generate questions is to take a thing and home in the bits of it that don't make sense, then you try to articulate the felt sense of the confusion, and what you would need to know in order to to resolve that confusion.
↓
1311576623888687104 [2020-10-01] @GeniesLoki 💜 9
There's also ur-questions like:

"How do these pieces fit together?" 
"What are recurring patterns here?"
"Which parts of this system are load bearing?"
"What would happen if you changed this bit?"

Infinite variations on these.
↓
1311576625671213056 [2020-10-01] @GeniesLoki 💜 6
I don't really know why I'm better at asking questions than most other people (that is, itself, an interesting question). Maybe it's native curiosity? It's probably at least partly trauma grounded. Confusing things feel unsafe and figuring out the right questions helps with that.
↓
1311576627135098880 [2020-10-01] @GeniesLoki 💜 8
Another way to cultivate question asking skills is to help your friends debug their emotions by asking them clarifying questions. I've done that a lot (which is totally not trauma grounded at all I just want everybody to be happy and love me for it perfectly normal instinct).
↓
1311576628582113282 [2020-10-01] @GeniesLoki 💜 6
Totally-just-jokes-because-I'm-very-healthy-and-untraumatised aside, question asking is a really useful skill and it's kinda weird that nobody teaches you to do it.
↓
1311576629995544576 [2020-10-01] @GeniesLoki 💜 7
Here's an exercise I like: Pick a random object in your environment and write a couple pages of observation about it.

There's a follow up you can do: What more is there to learn about this object? e.g. it's history, what it is it made of, etc. Can you come up with 100 questions?

title: The “shadow questions” thread that won’t die
summary:
GeniesLoki basically found a cheat code for involuntary self-therapy: “One like = one question you really wish I hadn’t asked you because of what your answer reveals about your shadow.” The very first one sets the tone—“Who in your personal life do you most hate and in what ways are you afraid that you are secretly like them?”—and the rest are variations on weaponizing shame, avoidance, and childhood authority dynamics to make you look straight at the stuff you’ve been dodging.

The arc is less “debate” and more “ritual artifact.” It kicks off in Sept 2020 with people immediately using it as a confessional tool: @visakanv posts a whole answered worksheet (worrying he’s secretly like a “narcissistic sociopath,” admitting “fear disguised as perfectionism” about shipping an ebook), while others reply like @zrkrlc: “yup i didn’t want to sleep tonight thank you very much.” The peak is when @nosilverv posts a DM coaching vignette where a friend goes from “i cry every time i try to make myself work out” to “Wtf why is my perspective now radically transformed… Why did this happen cuz a random bird account told me that part has knowledge,” and Nosilverv turns it into a pitch for how fast “inner work” can click when someone holds a better intention for you than you can hold for yourself.

Then instead of “dying,” it gets domesticated: GeniesLoki does meta threads explaining the ‘dirty secret’—it works because of *volume and coverage*, not mystical question-genius (“all I need… is clear a really low bar for success and get a good coverage of topics”). By 2021 it’s pinned, indexed, and proposed as a “Shadow Work Coloring Book” collab. By 2022, @DRMacIver is citing it as an example of “productive growth triggering done right.” And by 2025 you even get the skeptical counterpoint (@Oszillate) worrying the shadow concept invites randos to pretend they know you better than you do. Why care: it’s a rare Twitter thing that’s actually reusable—less hot-take machine, more crowdsourced prompt-engine that keeps resurfacing anytime people want to punch through their own self-deception.
